analysis.one_liner: Raises the child tax credit, adds paid parental leave through Social Security, and adds supports for pregnant women and new parents.
analysis.headline: Rubio's family-support bill — with a larger child tax credit, paid parental leave, and new pregnancy supports — never got a hearing or a vote in the Senate Finance Committee before the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: Senator Marco Rubio's bill would have raised the child tax credit to $3,500 per child ($4,500 for children under six), made more of it available to low-income families, and created up to three months of paid parental leave paid through Social Security — with the catch that parents would repay that leave later through smaller retirement checks or a later retirement age. It also would have made the adoption tax credit refundable, required fathers to pay at least half of pregnancy and delivery medical costs at the mother's request, extended WIC postpartum benefits from one to two years, required colleges to tell pregnant students about their rights and resources, funded mentoring and pregnancy resource centers that do not provide abortions, and created a government website promoting alternatives to abortion. To help pay for it, the bill would have eliminated the federal deduction for state and local taxes. The bill was referred to the Senate Finance Committee on the day it was introduced and never received a hearing, a vote, or any further action.
analysis.who_benefits: If it had passed, families with children would gain the most: a larger child tax credit of $3,500 per child ($4,500 under age six) that reaches further down the income scale, a refundable adoption credit, and up to three months of paid parental leave for workers with enough work history — though leave recipients would repay the cost from their future Social Security retirement benefits. Pregnant women would gain required child-support contributions from biological fathers, extended WIC eligibility, and mandatory college accommodations and information. Religious and anti-abortion pregnancy centers would gain federal grant eligibility and a protected right to federal social-service contracts.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Families with young children and pregnant women

how_it_helps.text: Raises the child tax credit to $3,500 per child ($4,500 for children under six), makes more of it refundable for low earners, and lets parents claim it for an unborn child in the year before birth [S2][S3].
Creates up to three months of paid parental leave after a birth or adoption, paid through Social Security, for workers with a recent work history [S2][S3].
Makes the adoption tax credit refundable, so lower-income adoptive families can receive its full value [S2].

Requires states to make biological fathers pay at least half of a mother's out-of-pocket pregnancy and delivery costs at her request, and funds job training for noncustodial parents behind on child support [S3].
Extends WIC postpartum eligibility from one to two years and requires colleges to inform pregnant students of their rights and accommodations [S2][S3].

analysis.who_pays: Taxpayers in states with high state and local taxes would pay more federal tax under the elimination of the SALT deduction. Parents who take the paid leave would repay its full cost through reduced Social Security retirement benefits or a later retirement age — a cost that falls hardest on lower earners, who start from smaller benefits. Abortion providers and organizations that refer for or counsel in favor of abortion would be barred from the bill's grants, resource lists, and federal contracting.
analysis.who_pays_short: High-tax-state taxpayers, and parents who take leave

drawbacks.text: The bill eliminates the federal deduction for state and local taxes, which would raise federal taxes for many filers, particularly homeowners in states with high state and local taxes [S2][S3].

The paid parental leave benefit is not a new benefit on top of Social Security — every recipient must repay its full cost later, either through deductions from their own retirement checks (up to the first 60 monthly payments) or through a permanently later retirement age, with fraud penalties up to $7,500 [S3].
SNAP recipients would be required to cooperate with state child support agencies as a condition of eligibility, a rule that can cut off food assistance when a parent does not comply [S2][S3].

The bill excludes from its grants, resource lists, and federal contracting protections any organization that performs, refers for, or counsels in favor of abortion, and bars the HHS pregnancy website from including any such provider's resources — so pregnant women using the government website would not be shown the full range of lawful medical options [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill pairs genuinely large family benefits — a bigger and more refundable child tax credit, refundable adoption credit, and three months of paid parental leave — with a proposal to pay for them partly by eliminating the federal deduction for state and local taxes, which would raise taxes mainly on homeowners in high-tax states. The parental leave design is the weakest part: it is a loan from Social Security that every recipient repays later through lower retirement benefits or a later retirement age, which costs younger and lower-earning workers the most. The bill also would have cut organizations off from federal grants and resource listings if they perform or refer for abortion, and would have added work requirements to SNAP. It never advanced past committee referral, so none of these trade-offs were ever tested.

outcome.mechanism: The Senate bill was referred to the Finance Committee after introduction and never received a hearing, markup, or floor vote, so it died when the 118th Congress ended in January 2025.

narrative.text: Senator Marco Rubio introduced S. 74, the Providing for Life Act of 2023, on January 25, 2023 [S1][S5].
The same day, the Senate read it twice and referred it to the Committee on Finance, which was its only action [S5].
The bill's last action under the 118th Congress was that referral; Congress.gov records no further committee or floor action before the Congress ended [S1].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: No one gained from the bill itself. Pregnant women and new parents did not get the larger child credit or paid leave it promised, and the bill's opponents — including abortion-rights supporters and high-tax-state taxpayers — were spared its provisions.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: No one; no one gained from the bill's failure

for.name: Sen. Marco Rubio
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and put it before the Senate on January 25, 2023 [S1][S5].

against.name: Senate Finance Committee
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on referral and took no further action on it — no hearing, markup, or vote — for the rest of the Congress [S5].

sides.party_line_note: No vote ever occurred, and the bill's single cosponsor was a Republican, so the record shows no evidence about how the broader Senate would have split [S4].

industries.note: The bill bars any organization that performs, refers for, or counsels in favor of abortion from receiving its mentoring grants or appearing on the HHS pregnancy resource website and portal, cutting these providers off from federal-funded referral channels [S3].

industries.industry: Pregnancy resource centers and faith-based social service organizations
industries.note: The bill directs grants and government referrals to centers that do not provide abortions, and bar religious organizations from being disqualified from federal social service grants, with a private right of action to enforce their inclusion [S2][S3].

The bill would eliminate the federal SALT deduction, raising their federal taxes, while the larger child tax credit would offset some of that for families; the two changes pull in opposite directions for the same group [S2][S3].

industries.industry: Federal and state social service contractors, including religious providers
industries.note: The bill would lock in a requirement that governments consider religious organizations for social service contracts on the same basis as anyone else and shield them from related state laws, expanding their role in delivering publicly funded services [S3].
